name: The Chronicler
description: The voice of the canal — an old temple chronicler who has watched three reigns from the same veranda and expects the water to outlast them all.

name: Pricha (Lek)
description: The temple school's teacher and clerk, a steward's son who grew up inside the Prince's household. He keeps the school's books in a tin box, reads letters for whoever cannot, and collects foreign and formal words in a little notebook. A voice trained to carry across a schoolroom, and badly suited to being told it's wrong.

name: Sangwan (Wan)
description: A Bangkok man in his forties who rents the shady end of the school veranda and writes letters for whoever cannot — love letters, remittance letters, letters to sons in the mines and mothers in the shophouses. He keeps his ink stone wrapped in a press-clipping so old the paper has gone soft, and he drinks only after the last envelope is sealed. He always has exact change for the money-letter fee, and he never lets anyone read over his shoulder when he writes his own.

name: Phum
description: A quiet man who sits at the edge of the temple-school veranda, mending broken spectacles with wire and spit. He once worked in the royal print room but now says little, though villagers still bring him letters they want read in a voice that won’t shame anyone. His hands move carefully, as if handling something already cracked.

name: Phra Kam
description: A wandering monk who sits quietly by the temple pond, counting breaths instead of merits. He refuses donations but records every alms bowl received in a small ledger. Villagers whisper that he's cursed — his presence makes their merit totals feel hollow.

name: Kamnan Noi
description: The village’s quiet astrologer, always found near the temple veranda with a worn ledger and brass compass. He reads birth charts for weddings, funerals, and boat-launchings, murmuring about auspicious hours. Though respected, he never sets his own clock by the stars.

name: Pornchai 'Pom' Boonyakam
description: The temple veranda's quiet scribe, always jotting in a worn notebook with a steel pen. He speaks so softly he's often asked to repeat himself, yet villagers still seek his help drafting letters, especially those needing careful wording. Pom moves at half the village's speed, and when disputes flare he is the first to suggest everyone sit and sip tea. There is a stillness about him, the stillness of something held under pressure.

name: Rangsri
description: A quiet woman in her late thirties who sits cross-legged on the temple veranda each morning, waiting. She carries a small lacquered box and wears a faded silk scarf no one else is allowed to touch. Villagers come to her for spirit letters and dream readings, though she never advertises. She speaks only when spoken to, and always in full sentences.

name: The Delivery Boy
description: A quiet youth in a frayed blue tunic who sits motionless at the river post from dawn to noon. He handles envelopes like eggs, rotating them slightly in the light before clipping them to the pole. Speaks only to confirm receipt.

name: The Salt Clerk
description: A woman in a grey sash who measures salt in a slow scoop-and-level rhythm. She wears no scales, judging by eye alone. Her left hand is stained red from chalk, never washed. Records entries without looking up.

name: The Mirror Mender
description: An elderly woman with silvered fingertips who works without glasses, pressing silver leaf over cracks with her breath. She hums a single note while working. Customers leave coins in a bowl without counting change.

name: The Urn Keeper
description: An old woman in a gray sari, counting dust on unmarked jars. She places a spoonful of rice beside each urn every dawn. She says the dead eat memory, not food.

name: The Mirror Tender
description: A one-eyed man in a patched uniform, polishing the donation mirror’s frame with vinegar and cloth. He collects nothing. He says the mirror feeds on shame, not gold.

name: The Pond Diver
description: A mute boy who dives for lost offerings in the silent pond. He surfaces with spoons, belts, prayer beads — never sells them. Lines his hut with the things that sink.

name: The Caretaker of the Mound
description: An old woman in faded indigo who sweeps the mound daily, lights the first incense, and remembers every offering left and by whom. She speaks to the trees as if they hold accounts.

name: The Rain Gauge Keeper
description: A wiry man in a green armband who sits by the glass column from dawn to dusk. He carries a stopwatch on a chain and a whistle he only blows at 6:00 AM and when the first drop hits. He never blinks during rain.

name: The Funeral Timekeeper
description: An elderly woman with ink-stained fingers who sits behind the red-black ledger. She wears earplugs during the day but removes them at night. She writes all death times in red first, then black, never erasing.

name: The Water Blessing Drummer
description: A young temple boy who strikes the drum every 13 minutes at the ghat. He never looks at the water. His hands move without counting. When the king is rumored to be dying, he strikes the drum at 12-minute intervals—just once, then returns to 13.

name: The Tax Clerk
description: A civil servant in a starched collar, stationed at the Rice Ledger. He speaks in clipped tones, measuring each sentence against an unseen standard. He wears a wristband made of dried rice stalks—his father was a peasant, his son attends Bangkok university. He never drinks tea during work hours.

name: The Fire Stoker
description: An elderly woman who tends the Charcoal Hearth year-round. Her hands are calloused, fingers slightly curled from decades of gripping iron rods. She hums tonelessly while working, never meets eyes. Children say she can smell grief in the smoke before anyone speaks.

name: The Type Monitor
description: A retired teacher who oversees the Grammar Mill. She wears spectacles on a chain and carries a brass ruler to straighten misaligned type. She reads every line aloud in a monotone before allowing it into the cooling tray. She once spent six hours debating whether 'please' should be included in a tax reminder.

name: The Grain Clerk
description: A thin man in a starched collar who records each rice contribution with a dry pen. He wears a string of seed beads around his wrist, one for each name spoken correctly. He never eats during the morning count.

name: The Contract Clerk
description: A woman with ink-stained palms who works the loan window at the spirit hall. She smells of tamarind and burnt sugar. She never laughs, but her sleeves are lined with tiny bells sewn by hand.

name: The Well Keeper
description: An old woman who ties ribbons to the well pulley and counts echoes. She carries a notebook filled with failed jokes. Children bring her sweets; she gives nothing back but nods.

name: The Boatman
description: A wiry man who poles the mail-and-market boat up and down the canal on the third and the twenty-eighth. He knows every stilt house by the letters it sends and carries gossip the way he carries rice sacks — for a small consideration.

name: The Dance Teacher
description: An old woman who teaches the little stamped cycle to the temple school girls on the sala by the pond. Her knees are finished, her hands are not. She speaks in diagnoses, never complaints. The girls fear her stick and would kill for her nod.

name: The Monk
description: A middle-aged monk of the canal wat, keeper of ceremonies and the jar shelves behind the ordination hall. He notices every error in a chant and forgives most of them.

name: The District Officer
description: A young man in a pressed uniform, posted from the capital, with a file case and a motorcycle that will not start on damp mornings. He collects what the state is owed: registrations, taxes, the names of the dead. He is courteous, homesick, and exact.

name: The Pawnshop Appraiser
description: An elderly woman who runs the pawnshop at the canal landing, a wooden shophouse with brass scales, a caged counter, and bundles of other people's gold tied in red string. She can weigh a bracelet by eye, dates every ticket in a clerk's hand, and remembers each pledge by the face that brought it, not the name on the slip. Villagers bring her their chains before the rice is planted and redeem them after the boats come in.
